title: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 17 Sep 2026]
    Title:A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Benchmark scores alone provide an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern artificial intelligence systems. Large language models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs) require different forms of assessment, yet their evaluation evidence must remain interpretable for development and oversight. We propose a unified framework that connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. The framework preserves system-specific metrics while mapping native measurements to common performance bands, accompanied by uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence. A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses, while safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from masking critical failures. Mappings to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements connect technical assessment with oversight needs. The framework provides a structured basis for assessing both system performance and the credibility of the evidence supporting it, with empirical validation across deployment contexts remaining an essential next step.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper proposes a unified framework to evaluate trustworthiness across LLMs, agentic AI, and multimodal systems using eight dimensions, meta-evaluation, and regulatory mappings.
report.background: AI evaluation has largely relied on benchmark scores, but these are fragmented and often fail to capture real-world trustworthiness. LLMs are assessed mainly on outputs, agentic systems add multi-step trajectories and tool use, and multimodal models require cross-modal reasoning checks. At the same time, regulators and standards bodies increasingly demand auditable evidence. The paper argues that benchmark scores alone are incomplete for development, deployment, and oversight. Its framework connects output-level, trajectory-level, and cross-modal assessment through eight dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. It also adds a meta-evaluation layer to judge whether the evaluation evidence itself is valid, reliable, and reproducible.
key_points: The framework defines eight trustworthiness dimensions: capability, robustness, safety, fairness, transparency, governance, oversight, and efficiency. It preserves system-specific metrics but maps native measurements to common performance bands, making LLM, agentic, and multimodal evaluations comparable without erasing important differences.

It links three assessment levels: output-level checks for LLM responses, trajectory-level checks for agentic systems that plan and use tools, and cross-modal checks for multimodal models. This addresses gaps where single-turn benchmarks miss long-horizon agent failures or vision-language inconsistencies.

A meta-evaluation layer examines the validity, reliability, and reproducibility of the evaluation itself. Results include uncertainty estimates and traceable evidence, helping developers and auditors understand not just what a system scored, but how credible that score is.

Safety-critical overrides prevent aggregate scores from hiding serious failures. Multidimensional profiles expose strengths and weaknesses across dimensions, so a system cannot appear trustworthy overall while failing dangerously in one area.

The framework maps to governance frameworks, international standards, and European Union regulatory requirements. The authors note that empirical validation across real deployment contexts remains an essential next step.
This is a conceptual and methodological proposal, not a fully validated benchmark. Its value depends on adoption, calibration, and testing against real systems and regulatory expectations.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the framework pushes evaluation from leaderboard chasing toward auditable, multidimensional evidence. Companies may need to document trajectories, uncertainty, and safety overrides, which could reshape model cards, procurement, and compliance workflows. For developers, it suggests tooling that tracks agent behavior, cross-modal consistency, and reproducibility, not just final answers. That adds engineering overhead but can catch failures earlier. For regular users, the payoff is safer and more transparent AI systems, especially as agents act autonomously. The risk is that complex evaluation frameworks become checkbox exercises or favor large labs able to afford rigorous testing. If validated, this approach could inform EU AI Act compliance and standardize how trust is measured.
report.tools: Watch evaluation projects such as EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness, Stanford HELM, UK AISI's Inspect AI, and MLCommons AI Safety for LLM trustworthiness. For agents, explore AgentBench, τ-bench, and SWE-bench; for multimodal, MMMU, MathVista, and OpenCompass. Promptfoo and DeepEval help developers add reproducible tests. These tools cover pieces of the proposed framework, though no single open-source project yet implements its full eight-dimension, meta-evaluation, and governance-mapping approach.
